## The Slutsk uprising, November–December 1920 {belarus soviet poland}

The demarcation line of the preliminary peace of 12 October placed most of Slutsk district on the side of Soviet Byelorussia. That autumn resolutions across Minsk Governorate called for "peacefully freeing Belarus from both Polish and Soviet troops". A report of the Belorussian Military Revolutionary Committee of 15 November stated that the population of some volosts recognised no authority but the non-existent government of "independent Belarus" and said that power should be elected, not appointed from Moscow. In Slutsk a Belarusian National Committee under Paval Zhavryd had been formed in 1918, and the Polish occupation authorities relied on this pro-Polish committee. Most supporters of independence gathered in the Slutsk committee of the Belarusian Party of Socialist-Revolutionaries, whose leaflets declared the partition of Belarusian lands between Poland and Soviet Russia illegal and Soviet Byelorussia's independence a fiction that "covers the occupation of the Belarusian people by Russian centralism". Russian-language sources describe peasants resisting War Communism as the main force, led by local intelligentsia and gentry. The congress of Slutsk district, which opened on 15 November, gathered 105 to 132 delegates, along with two officers of the Polish 11th Division and several representatives of Bułak-Bałachowicz's force. It proclaimed the authority of the Belarusian People's Republic in and around Slutsk, protested against "Bolshevik occupation" and elected a seventeen-member Slutsk Rada under the SR Uladzimir Prakulevich. [24](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BB%D1%83%D1%86%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B5_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5) [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slutsk_uprising) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic)

The Slutsk Rada declared a general mobilisation of men aged 16 to 50 and within three days formed the Slutsk Brigade of two regiments, the 1st Slutsk and the 2nd Hrozava; an account cited in Russian-language sources puts its strength at about 4,000. Belarusian historians disagree about where its arms and money came from: some say the Polish command supplied weapons and funds, others that only Bułak-Bałachowicz gave meagre help. The Polish Army left Slutsk on 24 November, and the brigade followed westwards and moved its headquarters to Semezhevo. Fighting began on 27 November. The insurgents beat the Red Army near Vasilchitsy and drove it out of Timkovichi, but the tide turned when the Red Army brought the 8th and 17th Divisions into the district. Driven from Semezhevo on 7 December, the insurgents retook it on the 12th together with large stocks of shells, but withdrew from Vyzna on the 19th and from Semezhevo on the 20th. They lacked arms, officers and food, and typhus broke out. On 28 December, out of ammunition, the brigade crossed the Morach River, now the border, laid down its arms and was interned by Poland. English-language sources note that the Red Army had to commit two divisions to overcome nearly a month of resistance. [24](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BB%D1%83%D1%86%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B5_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic)

The meaning of the uprising is still disputed. According to Russian-language sources the view most widely held among Belarusian academics treats it as a "myth": the area the Polish Army was to leave under the demarcation line had as yet neither Red Army troops nor Soviet authority, so there was no enemy to rise against, and the congress, without protesting that Western Belarus would stay in Poland, asked for Slutsk to be left on the Polish side. Anton Sokal-Kutyloŭski, who took over the brigade, flatly declared that "there was no uprising in Slutsk district", and Yury Listapad, a member of the Slutsk Rada, said he had gone to Warsaw for money allotted by the Polish General Staff. Other historians, by contrast, see it as the first independent armed struggle of Belarusians for their independence, fought under the slogan "Neither Polish lords nor Moscow communists". Since the national revival of the late 1980s the Belarusian Popular Front and others have marked 27 November as Heroes' Day, but Lukashenko's government does not regard the event as significant. Accounts of the exiled Rada's role also differ. English-language sources say the Rada, then in Lithuania, sent officers to help organise the resistance; Russian-language sources say historians have established no link between the insurgents and the Rada, while reporting that the Belarusian Military Rada sent 20 officers, of whom only three reached Slutsk. Vasil Bykaŭ's story On Black Slash-and-Burn Fields is set in these events. [24](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BB%D1%83%D1%86%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B5_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5) [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slutsk_uprising) [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_People's_Republic) [2](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%9D%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%A0%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%BF%D1%83%D0%B1%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0)

## The Treaty of Riga and the partition of Belarus {belarus poland soviet}

Peace talks opened in Minsk on 17 August 1920 and resumed in Riga on 21 September. Adolph Joffe led the Soviet delegation and Jan Dąbski the Polish. According to the sources on the Slutsk uprising, neither the Belarusian People's Republic nor Soviet Byelorussia was invited, and Soviet Russia signed on Soviet Byelorussia's behalf. According to the Belarusian historian Anatol Hrytskevich, Joffe offered Poland the whole of Soviet Byelorussia in exchange for territorial concessions in Ukraine, and the Poles declined. The Polish delegation was dominated by the National Democrats, Piłsudski's opponents, who did not want non-Polish minorities to exceed a third of the population; in the eastern countryside Ukrainians and Belarusians outnumbered Poles and voted for Piłsudski, so a border too far east would also hurt them at the polls. A special delegation of six Sejm deputies, under pressure from the National Democrat ideologue Stanisław Grabski, rejected some 100 kilometres of extra territory that would have put Minsk on the Polish side. English-language sources note that only at the Riga talks did Piłsudski or his allies seek to claim Minsk as the capital of a Belarusian People's Republic associated with Poland. In the end Minsk stayed Soviet. [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Riga) [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slutsk_uprising) [24](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BB%D1%83%D1%86%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B5_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5) [21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Soviet_War)

The Treaty of Riga was signed on 18 March 1921 between Poland on one side and Soviet Russia, acting also for Soviet Byelorussia, and Soviet Ukraine on the other. Poland recognised Soviet Ukraine and Soviet Byelorussia and undertook not to form federations with Lithuania, Belarus or Ukraine; the Soviet side renounced claims west of the line. The so-called Western Belarus, including the Grodno Governorate and the west of the Minsk Governorate, went to Poland. English-language sources place the new border some 200–250 kilometres east of the Curzon Line and count over a million Belarusians in the ceded areas; the Polish census of 1921 recorded about a million Belarusians, while some estimates run to 1.7–2 million. Article 7 guaranteed all nationalities free intellectual development, the use of their language and the exercise of their religion. What remained to Soviet Byelorussia was a small republic of 52,400 square kilometres and 1.544 million people; Gomel, Vitebsk and parts of Smolensk were administered by Russia. Belarusian activists saw the treaty as a tragic betrayal. Without Minsk, the Belarusians of Poland became a mostly rural, marginalised group, and to many of them the Soviet republic to the east looked like an attractive alternative. In the autumn of 1921 a congress of Belarusian representatives in Prague condemned the partition and adopted a resolution to fight for the unification of Belarus. [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Riga) [27](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A0%D0%B8%D0%B6%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%80_%281921%29) [21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Soviet_War) [16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Belorussia) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic)

Soviet Byelorussia's status was settled afterwards. On 16 January 1921 Russia and Byelorussia concluded a Union Workers' and Peasants' Treaty recognising each other's independence and sovereignty, and on 30 December 1922 the republic became a founding member of the Soviet Union. English-language sources explain that its small territory and weak national sentiment would have made absorption into Russia unremarkable, but for Leon Trotsky and other advocates of world revolution, who saw Riga as a temporary setback, the republic was a bridgehead for a future advance west and a magnet for the minorities of Poland, and so it received the status of a full union republic. In March 1924 Russia handed over most of the Vitebsk and Mogilev governorates and parts of Smolensk, doubling its area to 110,600 square kilometres and raising its population to 4.2 million. In the 1920s the Soviet Union supported Belarusian culture, founding national institutions and thousands of Belarusian schools, though most of this was destroyed under Stalin in the 1930s. In Western Belarus, Belarusian deputies in the Polish Sejm founded the Belarusian Peasants' and Workers' Hramada in 1925, demanding self-government for Western Belarus, recognition of Belarusian as a second official language and an end to "colonisation" by Polish settlers; the party received help from the Soviet Union and money from the Comintern. [11](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BE%D1%86%D0%B8%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B8%D1%87%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%A1%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%A0%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%BF%D1%83%D0%B1%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0_%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D1%81%D0%B8%D1%8F) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic) [21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Soviet_War) [28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_Peasants'_and_Workers'_Union)

## The Rada in exile, the aftermath and assessments {belarus}

From 1919 the Rada of the Belarusian People's Republic was a body in exile. After the Polish Sejm ratified the annexation of the Vilnius region in March 1922, Lithuania lost interest in the Rada and stopped funding it, and in November 1923 the government left Kaunas for Prague; Lastouski gave up the premiership that year. When the Soviet side transferred more Belarusian land to Soviet Byelorussia in 1924, pro-Soviet feeling grew in Western Belarus and among the émigrés. At the Second Belarusian Political Conference in Berlin in October 1925 the government headed by Cvikievič handed its powers to the government of Soviet Byelorussia, recognised Minsk as the sole cultural and political centre and dissolved itself. The Rada's chairman, Piotra Krečeŭski, rejected this as a "betrayal of independence", and the Rada stayed in exile without ever recognising Soviet Byelorussia. Those who went back met tragic fates. Lastouski, who moved to Soviet Byelorussia in 1927 and became director of the State Museum and an academician, was arrested in 1930 in the case of the "Union for the Liberation of Belarus" and exiled to Saratov, then rearrested in 1937 and executed in January 1938. Jan Sierada, working in agriculture in Soviet Byelorussia, was arrested in the same case in 1930 and passed through exile and the Gulag; his fate after his release in 1943 is unknown. Zmicier Zhylunovich, a communist, was arrested in 1936 and died in a psychiatric hospital in Mogilev in 1937. [2](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%9D%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%A0%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%BF%D1%83%D0%B1%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0) [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_People's_Republic) [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rada_of_the_Belarusian_Democratic_Republic) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatslaw_Lastowski) [14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Sierada) [18](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%96%D0%B8%D0%BB%D1%83%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87,_%D0%94%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%82%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%A4%D1%91%D0%B4%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87)

Those who stayed in Western Belarus were not safe either. Anton Luckievič revived Nasha Niva in Vilnius and led Belarusian school and museum work, but in 1927 the Polish authorities arrested him on charges of working with German and Soviet intelligence; he was acquitted. In the 1930s the publishing society he headed was banned, and in Soviet Byelorussia a 1937 order required his books to be burned. When the Soviet Union occupied Western Belarus in 1939 he was arrested in Vilnius, sentenced to eight years, and died in 1942 while being transferred to a camp. On the Soviet side, Alexander Myasnikov went on to head the government of Soviet Armenia and died in a plane crash near Tbilisi in 1925. The exiled Rada spent the Second World War in Prague; sources differ in judging its chairman Vasil Zacharka's dealings with Nazi Germany. After the war the Rada continued its work in the West. When Belarus declared sovereignty in 1990 the Rada said it was ready to hand its status to a democratically elected parliament, but dropped the idea after Alexander Lukashenko came to power in 1994. Unlike the exile governments of its neighbours, which handed over their mandates, the Rada remains the oldest existing government in exile. [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Luckievich) [9](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9C%D1%8F%D1%81%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B2,_%D0%90%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D1%80_%D0%A4%D1%91%D0%B4%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87) [8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Miasnikian) [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_People's_Republic) [2](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D1%81%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%9D%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B4%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%A0%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%BF%D1%83%D0%B1%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0) [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rada_of_the_Belarusian_Democratic_Republic)

How to judge Belarusian state-building in these years depends on the camp. The Bolsheviks branded the Belarusian People's Republic an attempt by bourgeois and landlord circles to tear Belarus away from Russia, and Vladimir Lenin called the Hramada a "nationalist petty-bourgeois party of left-populist orientation"; the Second Congress of Soviets of the Western Oblast declared the Rada counter-revolutionary and anti-Soviet. Russian-language sources point out that the republic did not manage to become a real state in its short life and that the idea of an independent state based on national sovereignty did not win the support of the whole population of the Belarusian lands. Since the late 1980s, by contrast, the Belarusian national-democratic opposition has celebrated 25 March as Freedom Day and treats the republic as the starting point of an independent state. Soviet historians counted the proclamation of 1 January 1919 as the first founding of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, and according to Russian-language sources Belarusian historiography also treats it as a continuation of modern Belarusian statehood. The scholar Tania Raffass observed that both states owed their almost "unsolicited" existence to the competing German, Russian and Polish attempts to control the area. The border drawn at Riga lasted until the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939.
