1918년 여름 동카렐리야 곳곳에서 핀란드 편입 청원이 들어왔고, 특히 투표로 편입을 결의한 레폴라가 적극적이었다. 핀란드군은 가을 레폴라를 점령했고, 러시아어 출처는 그 날짜를 10월 15일로 적는다. 1919년 1월에는 작은 의용대가 포라얘르비를 점령했다가 볼셰비키군에 곧 밀려났다. 2월 만네르헤임은 서방 열강과 러시아 백군에게 물질적·정신적 지원이 있으면 핀란드가 페트로그라드의 볼셰비키를 공격하겠다고 밝혔고, 같은 무렵 아우누스(올로네츠 카렐리야) 원정이 준비되었다. 지휘관 군나르 폰 헤르첸은 카렐리야 주민이 함께 싸운다면 의용병 1,000명으로 충분하다고 보았다. 원정대 1,000명은 4월 21일 밤 국경을 넘어 로데이노예폴레, 페트로자보츠크, 무르만스크 철도를 노렸고, 23일 올로네츠를 차지해 한때 페트로자보츠크를 위협했다. 그러나 병력은 모자랐고 카렐리야인 자원자는 적었다. 의용병 2,000명을 새로 모집하고 지휘관도 아르네 시흐보로 바꾸었지만, 6월 20일 파보 탈벨라의 연대가 페트로자보츠크를 공격했다가 붉은 군대와 핀란드 적위대에 패했다. 6월 26일 페트로그라드 적색 장교학교의 핀란드인 600여 명이 라도가 호수를 건너 비텔레에 상륙해 핀란드군의 배후를 치자 원정대는 큰 손실을 입고 물러났다. 남은 성과는 6월 포라얘르비가 핀란드 편입을 선언하고 정규군이 이를 점령한 것뿐이었다. 같은 7월 카렐리야 지협 남쪽에서는 잉그리아 핀란드인 피란민이 북잉그리아(키르야살로) 공화국을 선포했지만, 30제곱킬로미터 남짓한 땅에 머물렀다. 핀란드 의용병은 바다 건너 에스토니아로도 갔다. 마르틴 에크스트룀이 이끈 제1핀란드 의용군단에 이어, 한스 칼름이 모집한 「북방의 아들들(포흐얀 포야트)」 2,213명과 관리 400명이 1919년 1월 12일 핀란드만을 건넜다. 위원회가 정한 상한은 1,000명이었지만 칼름은 이를 무시했다. 이들은 1월 31일 파주 전투에 투입되었고, 2월에는 국경을 넘어 라트비아의 마리엔부르크까지 진격했다. 에스토니아 쪽의 전쟁은 발트 독립전쟁 사건에서 다룬다. 정작 페트로그라드로는 끝내 가지 않았다. 만네르헤임은 핀란드 백군의 승리를 러시아 전체의 반볼셰비키 투쟁의 일부로 보았지만, 진격의 조건으로 권위 있는 러시아 정부가 핀란드 독립을 승인해야 한다고 했다. 알렉산드르 콜차크는 6월 4일 연합국에 보낸 전보에서 핀란드 독립을 사실상으로만 인정하고 법적 승인은 장래의 제헌의회에 맡기겠다고 답했다. 러시아어 출처에 따르면 만네르헤임은 6월 18일 핀란드에 와 있던 니콜라이 유데니치와 비밀 협정을 맺었지만 실제 결과로 이어지지 않았다. 대통령 선거를 앞두고 사회민주당 언론은 콜차크 정부의 모호한 태도를 들어 만네르헤임과 「백색 러시아」의 친분이 독립을 위협한다고 공격했다. 스톨베리는 소비에트 러시아와의 강화를 지지했고, 7월 선거에서 이겼다. 10월 유데니치의 북서군이 페트로그라드 앞까지 갔을 때 만네르헤임은 백군이 지면 그 책임이 핀란드에 있을 것이라고 썼지만, 그는 이미 공직에서 물러나 있었다. ## 1920년 타르투 조약과 그 뒤 {finland soviet}

1920년 동쪽의 사정은 크게 바뀌었다. 연합군이 1919년 가을 북러시아에서 철수하고 백군이 무너지자, 우흐투아에서 백해 카렐리야의 독립을 결의한 카렐리야 임시정부는 5월 붉은 군대에 쫓겨 핀란드로 달아났다. 6월 8일 페트로자보츠크에서 러시아 소비에트 연방 사회주의 공화국의 자치주인 카렐리야 노동 코뮌이 세워졌다. 그 구상에는 에드바르드 귈링이 있었다. 스톡홀름에서 핀란드 공산당 사무국을 이끌던 그는 5월 레닌의 초청으로 모스크바에 가서 카렐리야 자치 공화국의 가능성을 보고했다. 북쪽에서는 1월 예브게니 밀레르가 끊긴 전신선을 다시 이어 달라고 요청한 것을 명분으로 발레니우스의 원정대가 다시 페차모로 들어갔으나, 3월 22일 소비에트군의 상륙 공세에 밀려 노르웨이 쪽으로 물러났다. 7월 붉은 군대는 동카렐리야 대부분에서 핀란드군을 밀어냈고, 핀란드군은 레폴라와 포라얘르비에만 남았다. 6월 타르투에서 시작된 협상에서 핀란드 대표단은 유호 쿠스티 파시키비가 이끌었고 배이뇌 탄네르, 배이뇌 보이온마, 루돌프 발덴 등이 참여했다. 소비에트 대표단에는 플라톤 케르젠체프 등이 있었다. 러시아어 출처에 따르면 외무장관 루돌프 홀스티는 라도가 호수에서 오네가 호수를 거쳐 백해에 이르는 선을 원했지만, 파시키비는 주민 스스로 원하는 땅만 합쳐야 한다고 보았다. 핀란드는 동카렐리야 주민투표를 제안했으나 소비에트의 반대로 거두어들였다. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petsamo_expeditions) [37](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%82%D1%83%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%80_%D0%BC%D0%B5%D0%B6%D0%B4%D1%83_%D0%A0%D0%A1%D0%A4%D0%A1%D0%A0_%D0%B8_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B5%D0%B9) [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29)

거의 다섯 달의 협상 끝에 10월 14일 타르투의 에스토니아 학생회 건물에서 조약이 서명되었다. 국경은 옛 핀란드 대공국과 러시아 제국의 경계를 따랐다. 핀란드는 북극해의 얼지 않는 항구가 있는 페차모를 얻었다. 1864년 알렉산드르 2세가 카렐리야 지협의 땅과 맞바꾸어 핀란드에 주기로 약속했던 곳이다. 그 대신 핀란드는 비에나 원정과 아우누스 원정 뒤 합병해 점령했던 레폴라와 포라얘르비를 돌려주고 1921년 2월 14일까지 군대를 빼기로 했으며, 북잉그리아도 러시아에 넘겼다. 이 대가로 소비에트 측은 동카렐리야의 문화적 자치를 약속했다. 소비에트는 라도가 호수의 핀란드 항구에서 네바강을 거쳐 핀란드만으로 가는 핀란드 상선의 자유 항행을 보장했고, 핀란드는 페차모를 거쳐 노르웨이로 가는 육상 통과를 보장했다. 핀란드는 크론시타트 맞은편 이노 요새의 무장을 풀고 핀란드만의 바깥 섬들을 비무장화하기로 했다. 러시아어 출처에 따르면 러시아 소비에트 연방 사회주의 공화국 중앙집행위원회가 10월 23일, 핀란드 의회가 12월 1일 조약을 승인했고, 스톨베리 대통령이 12월 11일 비준했다. 비준서는 12월 31일 모스크바에서 교환되었다. 이 조약은 같은 해 2월 에스토니아가 같은 도시에서 소비에트 러시아와 맺은 타르투 조약과는 별개다. 핀란드 의회의 민족주의 우파는 대핀란드의 꿈을 버린 조약을 수치스럽다고 했지만, 파시키비는 뒷날 이 국경이 영구히 유지되기에는 핀란드에 지나치게 좋았다고 인정했다. [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29) [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petsamo_expeditions) [31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunus_expedition) [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [37](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%82%D1%83%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%80_%D0%BC%D0%B5%D0%B6%D0%B4%D1%83_%D0%A0%D0%A1%D0%A4%D0%A1%D0%A0_%D0%B8_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B5%D0%B9)

조약 뒤에도 동쪽 국경은 조용하지 않았다. 핀란드 외무부가 레폴라와 포라얘르비 주민의 무장을 막으라고 지시하자, 레폴라의 젊은 경찰서장 보비 시벤은 1921년 1월 12일 핀란드가 동카렐리야인을 「배신」했다는 유서를 남기고 자살했다. 약속된 자치가 제대로 이행되지 않고 식량난이 겹치자 1921년 가을 동카렐리야 분리주의자들이 봉기했고, 약 550명의 핀란드 의용병이 주로 장교와 분대장으로 가담했다. 핀란드 정부는 공식 개입은 거부했지만 의용병의 월경을 막지 않았고, 소비에트 측은 이를 정부의 군사 개입으로 보았다. 붉은 군대 약 2만 명이 반격해 1922년 2월까지 봉기를 진압했고, 동카렐리야 피란민 약 3만 명이 핀란드로 건너왔다. 러시아에서는 1918~1920년의 원정과 1921~1922년의 충돌을 소련-핀란드 전쟁의 하나로 보지만, 핀란드 역사학은 이 원정들을 러시아와의 전쟁으로 치지 않는다. 카렐리야 노동 코뮌은 1923년 카렐리야 자치 소비에트 사회주의 공화국이 되었고, 귈링은 1935년까지 그 인민위원회의 의장으로 핀란드어 중심의 정책을 폈다. 핀란드인이 소수인 지역에서 북미와 핀란드의 이주자를 불러들인 이 정책은 1930년대 「민족주의적 쇼비니즘」으로 비난받았고, 귈링은 1935년 물러나 1938년 처형되었다. 에로 하팔라이넨도 1937년 페트로자보츠크에서 총살되었다. 타르투가 그은 국경은 1939년 소련이 겨울전쟁을 일으켜 조약을 깨뜨릴 때까지 유지되었다. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Haapalainen) [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29)

이 전쟁은 이름부터가 해석이다. 전쟁 중에는 양쪽 모두 「독립전쟁(바파우소타)」이라는 말을 썼다. 적색에게는 자본주의로부터의 해방, 백색에게는 소비에트 러시아의 영향으로부터의 자유라는 뜻이었다. 적색과 그 지지자들은 「계급전쟁」과 「혁명」을, 백색은 「적색 반란」을 썼으며, 패전 뒤 재건된 사회민주당은 점점 「내전」이라는 말을 썼다. 2008년 일간지 아물레흐티의 조사에서 응답자 1,005명은 「내전」 29퍼센트, 「시민전쟁」 25퍼센트, 「계급전쟁」 13퍼센트, 「독립전쟁」 11퍼센트, 「적색 반란」 5퍼센트를 골랐다. 영어 출처는 인구 약 300만 가운데 3만 5천~3만 8천 명이 죽고 고아 약 1만 5천 명이 생겼다고 보며, 죽음의 대부분은 전장이 아니라 수용소와 테러에서 나왔다. 사회는 「두 나라의 시민」으로 갈렸고, 백군은 「도살자(라흐타리)」로, 적색은 「적색 러시아인(푸니키)」으로 불렸다. 1950년대까지 주류 문학은 승자의 관점을 따랐고, 적색의 이야기는 1959~1962년 배이뇌 린나의 3부작 『북극성 아래에서』 이후에야 널리 쓰였다. 화해는 느리게 왔다. 퀴외스티 칼리오는 1918년 5월 5일 니발라 연설에서 적색과 백색으로 나뉘지 않은 민족을 다시 세우자고 호소했고, 배이뇌 보이온마는 1919년 이 나라가 전쟁으로 거의 모든 것을 잃었다고 탄식했다. 영어 출처는 적색의 패배와 백색 목표 대부분의 좌절, 독일과 러시아의 동시 약화가 핀란드식 타협의 바탕이 되었다고 본다. 반면 망명 지도자들은 1918년 8월 29일 모스크바에서 핀란드 공산당을 세웠고, 수용소의 고통은 핀란드 안의 공산주의 지지를 키웠다. ## From grand duchy to independence: 1917 {finland russia}

A grand duchy of the Russian Empire since 1809, Finland was an autonomous state with its own budget and its own currency, the markka. After Russification began in 1899, however, the Tsar repeatedly dissolved the parliament between 1908 and 1917 and appointed the Senate as he pleased. The 1906 reform had nonetheless created a unicameral parliament elected by universal suffrage, women included, and the Social Democratic Party had become, relative to population, larger than any other socialist party in the world. When the February Revolution removed Nicholas II, the Russian Provisional Government's manifesto of 15 March restored the autonomy of 1809–1899. Oskari Tokoi of the Social Democrats, who had won an absolute majority in 1916, formed a Senate in March of six Social Democrats and six non-socialists, the world's first social democratic head of government. Power, however, slipped into the streets. Grain imports from southern Russia stopped, food shortages, unemployment and inflation piled up, and strikes for the eight-hour day and higher wages swept industry and farms. In July parliament passed the Power Act with the votes of the Social Democrats, the Agrarian League and others: all legislative power except foreign and military affairs lay with parliament, which alone could dissolve itself. The Regional Committee of the Finnish Soviets, led by the Bolshevik Ivar Smilga, promised to defend the parliament if it were attacked. But the Provisional Government survived the July Days, refused to accept the Act and, with the cooperation of Finnish conservatives, dissolved the parliament and sent more Russian troops. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Declaration_of_Independence) [3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskari_Tokoi)

In the elections of 1–2 October the Social Democrats gained votes but lost their absolute majority, and the non-socialist parties together won more than half the seats. The defeat radicalised the labour movement. When the Bolsheviks took power in Petrograd on 7 November, the Finnish parliament adopted a compromise put forward by the Agrarian leader Santeri Alkio: on 15 November it assumed supreme power on the basis of the Power Act and ratified the eight-hour day and universal suffrage in local elections. The same day the Soviet government proclaimed the right of the peoples of Russia to self-determination, including complete secession. On 1 November the Social Democrats had issued their programme We Demand, calling for a return to the situation before the July dissolution, the disbanding of the Civil Guards and elections to a constituent assembly; when it was rejected they called a general strike for 14–19 November. The strike leadership voted narrowly for revolution on the 16th, then called it off the same day for lack of activists to carry it out. Lenin and Stalin were urging the Finnish Social Democrats to take power, and according to Russian-language sources Joseph Stalin, the People's Commissar for Nationalities, addressed the party congress in Helsinki in person on 14 November. Most Finnish socialists, however, were moderates who preferred parliamentary methods, and the Bolsheviks called them "reluctant revolutionaries". During the strike the Finnish Red Guards executed several political opponents in the south and the first armed clashes took place; 34 people died. On 27 November the purely non-socialist Senate of Pehr Evind Svinhufvud was appointed, with the aims of separating Finland from Russia and strengthening the Civil Guards. [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1917_Finnish_parliamentary_election) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Declaration_of_Independence) [5](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%93%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%B9%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%B2_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B8)

Svinhufvud's Senate laid the declaration of independence and a bill for a republican form of government before parliament on 4 December, and parliament adopted the declaration on 6 December. The Social Democrats voted against the Senate's text and offered their own declaration of sovereignty, but both camps supported independence as such. The conservatives hurried secession in order to contain the left and limit Bolshevik influence; the socialists distrusted sovereignty under conservative rule but feared losing nationalist workers. Independence still needed Russia's recognition. The socialists, who had been reluctant to negotiate with the Russian leadership in July, now sent two delegations to Petrograd to ask Lenin for it. Under heavy German pressure at Brest-Litovsk, Vladimir Lenin calculated that the Bolsheviks could hold the centre of Russia but had to give up peripheral territories such as Finland in the north-western corner. On the night of 31 December Svinhufvud's delegation received the Sovnarkom's decision recognising independence at the Smolny; Lenin, after an embarrassed refusal, came out into the corridor and shook Svinhufvud's hand. The All-Russian Central Executive Committee approved the decision on 4 January 1918. Soviet Russia was the first government outside Finland to recognise its independence. By the outbreak of the civil war Germany, Sweden, France, Austria-Hungary and others had followed, but Britain and the United States held back, watching Finland's ties with Germany. English-language sources explain that the Bolsheviks also hoped a communist revolution would one day bring Finland back to them. [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Declaration_of_Independence) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pehr_Evind_Svinhufvud) [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustaf_Emil_Mannerheim)

## Two armed camps: Red Guards and Civil Guards {finland}

The February Revolution dissolved the Finnish police, and in the vacuum both right and left set up their own security groups. At first they were local and largely unarmed, but by late 1917, with parliament dissolved and no strong government or national army, they became increasingly paramilitary. On the right, conservative academics, industrialists, major landowners and activists organised the Civil Guards (suojeluskunnat), later called the White Guards. Their number grew from 149 on 31 August 1917 to 251 at the end of September, 315 at the end of October, 380 at the end of November and 408 on 26 January 1918. In September a 200-strong cavalry school was set up on the Saksanniemi estate near Porvoo. There was also the Jäger battalion of some 1,900 Finnish volunteers trained in Germany in 1915–1917; its vanguard and German weapons arrived in October–November aboard a freighter and the German submarine UC-57, and around 50 Jägers were back by the end of the year. On the left, Workers' Order Guards were recruited through local Social Democratic branches and trade unions, and a minority of them were Red Guards in the tradition of 1905–1906. After the election defeat, the labour movement called on 20 October for more units, and the guards multiplied to 100–150 at the end of October, 342 at the end of November and 375 on 26 January 1918. Yet even the largest guard in Helsinki had only 20–30 military rifles. The coexistence of two armed forces split society into a state of dual power, and the decisive break came during the general strike. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards_%28Finland%29)

The Russian army was still in Finland too. In January 1918 about 50,000 troops of the former Tsarist army were stationed there, demoralised, war-weary peasants hungry for the land the revolution had freed; most of them returned to Russia by the end of March. In early January the Red Guard commander-in-chief Ali Aaltonen went to Petrograd to buy weapons. There he took to drinking and for a while nobody knew where he was; on 13 January the Red Guard staff decided to fill his post quickly, but the same day Aaltonen reported that 10,000 rifles and 10 field guns would arrive within a few weeks. At the same time the Civil Guards were preparing to receive 60,000 rifles from Germany. The first local battles were fought between 9 and 21 January in southern and south-eastern Finland, mostly in the arms race and for control of Viipuri; at Taavetti station in Luumäki the Civil Guards seized 200 rifles. On 12 January parliament authorised the Svinhufvud Senate to establish order, and on 15 January Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, a former general of the Imperial Russian Army, was appointed commander-in-chief of the Civil Guards, which the Senate designated as Finland's White Army. Mannerheim set up his headquarters in the Vaasa–Seinäjoki area on the west coast, issued the order to engage on the 25th, and obtained weapons by disarming the Russian garrisons of southern Ostrobothnia on 21–28 January. According to Russian-language sources the Russian garrisons in the north put up almost no resistance. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Aaltonen) [8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards_%28Finland%29) [5](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%93%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%B9%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%B2_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B8)

## 27–28 January 1918: Finland split in two {finland}

The Red Guards refused to accept White supremacy and set up a military authority of their own. Aaltonen established his headquarters in Helsinki and nicknamed it Smolna, after the Bolsheviks' Smolny. The Red order of revolution was issued on 26 January, and a red lantern, the signal of the rising, was lit in the tower of the Helsinki Workers' House. The Helsinki Red Guard and some units along the Viipuri–Tampere railway had been activated on 23–26 January to secure key points and escort a heavy shipment of Bolshevik weapons from Petrograd, and mass mobilisation began late on the 27th. Whites trying to seize the shipment clashed with Reds at Kämärä on the Karelian Isthmus that day, and 20–30 Finns died. On the 28th the Red Guards took control of Helsinki. The same day Social Democrats set up a revolutionary government against the Senate, the Finnish People's Delegation, chaired by Kullervo Manner, party chairman and Speaker of Parliament in 1917. Edvard Gylling took finance, Otto Wille Kuusinen education and Oskari Tokoi supply. Eero Haapalainen, a trade union leader without military training, replaced Aaltonen as commander-in-chief that day and joined the Delegation. The Delegation was supervised by the Central Workers' Council, and locally workers' councils replaced the old municipal authorities, keeping order, rationing food and running workplaces. But senior and middle-ranking officials of the old administration refused to cooperate, and new staff had to be chosen and trained from among junior clerks. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Socialist_Workers'_Republic) [9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Aaltonen) [11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Haapalainen) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullervo_Manner)

The leaders of Red Finland envisaged a path different from Lenin's dictatorship of the proletariat. Kuusinen's draft constitution of 23 February, influenced by the Swiss and American constitutions and the French Revolution, concentrated power in parliament with a lesser role for the government. It provided for a multi-party system, freedom of assembly, speech and the press, and wide use of referendums; to safeguard the labour movement it gave the people a right to "permanent revolution", and it would have transferred much of property to the state and local administrations. The concept of the dictatorship of the proletariat was absent. The draft was never finalised, however, and in practice a regime born of revolution and civil war leaned on violence, including political terror. The socialists themselves had to ask whether power won by revolution could give democracy a real chance, since restoring the strength they had held in parliament until July 1917 was one of the main aims of the January revolution. On territory, too, Red Finland did not abandon nationalism. Most Reds wanted a neutral, independent Finland, and some demanded that Aunus, Viena Karelia and Petsamo be joined to it. Only the Finnish Bolsheviks, few but influential in the Red Guards, supported annexation by Russia. Expansionists in the White camp coveted the same lands, so a Greater Finland was a dream shared across the divide. [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Socialist_Workers'_Republic) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War)

The government of White Finland was Svinhufvud's Senate, called the Vaasa Senate because it made the west-coast town of Vaasa its capital from 29 January to 3 May. Svinhufvud himself hid in Helsinki, sending pleas for intervention to Germany and Sweden, before escaping to Vaasa via Berlin and Stockholm in March. According to Russian-language sources, Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg, Kyösti Kallio and other politicians stayed hidden in Helsinki until the Germans arrived. Between 28 January and 3 February a front line running east–west across southern Finland took shape and changed little until the White offensive in March. The Red Guards held the south, with nearly all the large towns and industrial centres and the big estates with the most crofters and tenant farmers. The Whites held the agrarian north, with small and medium farms and crofters of better standing. Each side held enclaves behind the other's lines, such as the industrial towns of Varkaus, Kuopio and Oulu in White territory and Porvoo in Red territory. Each side fielded 70,000–90,000 Finns, with around 100,000 rifles and 300–400 machine guns. The Red Guards were mainly volunteers paid wages at first and included 2,600 women; the White Army was mostly conscripts, with 11,000–15,000 volunteers. Urban and rural workers made up most of the Red Guards, landowning farmers and the educated the backbone of the White Army. When the Whites began conscription in February, 30,000 labour supporters never reported. Both sides used boy soldiers aged 14 to 17. ## Soviet Russia and Red Finland {finland russia soviet}

Soviet Russia supplied weapons and some men, but fewer men than is often assumed. Some 4,000–5,000 Red Russian soldiers supported the Finnish Reds, but only about 3,000, in separate small units of 100–1,000, fought at the front. Russian officers were divided. Mikhail Svechnikov led Finnish Red troops in western Finland in February and Konstantin Yeremeyev commanded Soviet forces on the Karelian Isthmus, while other officers, distrusting their revolutionary peers, cooperated with Mannerheim in disarming Russian garrisons. On 30 January Mannerheim told the Russian soldiers in Finland that the White Army was not fighting Russia but the Finnish Reds and the Soviet troops helping them. White propaganda nonetheless painted the war as a defensive struggle against Russian Bolsheviks and played down the Finns among the enemy. Weapons mattered more. In early February a train commanded by Jukka Rahja arrived from Petrograd with 15,000 rifles, machine guns, artillery and 2 million cartridges that Aaltonen had bought from the Bolsheviks. According to Russian-language sources, Lenin had promised military help as early as 13 January. The Reds also flew aircraft, but having no Finnish pilots they relied mostly on Russians, and poor command, fuel and maintenance kept their air effort ineffective. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards_%28Finland%29) [5](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%93%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%B9%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%B2_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B8)

On 1 March the People's Delegation and the Sovnarkom signed a treaty in Petrograd, Lenin and Stalin for the Soviet side, Edvard Gylling and Oskari Tokoi for the Finnish. The name "Finnish Socialist Workers' Republic" appears only in this treaty: the Delegation had been using "Republic of Finland", Lenin proposed adding "Socialist Workers' Republic" during the talks, and the Delegation later blamed its negotiators, saying the Finns themselves should have chosen the name. Gylling, the prime mover of the talks, hoped to reduce Russian influence in Finland and open the way to peace talks with White Finland. The negotiations showed that even between two socialist governments nationalism counted for more than international socialism. There were major disputes over the border between Red Finland and Soviet Russia; the Finns obtained Petsamo, but Aunus and Viena were left open. According to English-language sources Lenin, who had stressed self-determination before the revolution, leaned towards federalism once in power and expected Finland eventually to be joined to Russia. The treaty lost its significance quickly when the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed two days later. Both unstable socialist states were absorbed in their own civil wars, and the fate of Red Finland was decided by power politics between Russia and Germany. [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Socialist_Workers'_Republic) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskari_Tokoi) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War)

When Germany resumed its attack on Russia on 18 February, the number of Soviet soldiers fighting in Finland fell sharply. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of 3 March required Russian forces to leave Finland, and Bolshevik support was restricted to weapons and supplies. According to Russian-language sources, after the German Foreign Office protested on 30 March that Red Guards from Petrograd were still crossing into Finland in large groups, Lenin on 1 April forbade the official dispatch of troops to help the People's Delegation. Soviet units nonetheless fought on the Karelian Isthmus in the Battle of Rautu from February to April, defending the approaches to the capital. The Baltic Fleet left Helsinki too. Moved there from Tallinn on Lenin's orders in February, it broke through the ice with the help of icebreakers before the Germans arrived, and all its ships had reached Kronstadt and Petrograd by 22 April; they later played an important part in the defence of Petrograd. Pro-Red Russian troops still in Helsinki took no part in the battle for the city, in accordance with the treaty. On 11 May, at German insistence, some 2,100 former Russian subjects remaining in Helsinki were expelled. English-language sources judge that by agreeing at Brest not to meddle in the Finnish war, the Bolsheviks left the Finnish communists without the aid they had been promised. Russia's withdrawal in effect handed Red Finland's fate to Germany. ## The Battle of Tampere {finland}

From February to early March the Red Guards mounted a general offensive along the front, but a chronic lack of skilled leaders left most attacks fruitless; field commanders were often elected by their men, and training and discipline were poor. On 20 March Haapalainen was removed as commander-in-chief after a series of defeats and replaced by the Bolshevik triumvirate of Eino Rahja, Adolf Taimi and Evert Eloranta. The Whites had two advantages: a professional command of Mannerheim, 84 Swedish volunteer officers and Finnish officers of the former Tsarist army, and 1,450 Jägers, most of whom arrived in Vaasa on 25 February. Hardened on the Eastern Front, the Jägers began rapid training of six conscript regiments at the end of February; 450 Jägers considered likely to side with the Reds were left in Germany. Mannerheim weighed whether to strike first at the industrial town of Tampere or at Viipuri, Karelia's main city, and judging Viipuri too risky he chose Tampere, a workers' town held by some 15,000 armed Red Guards. On 16 March he launched the main assault through the right flank of the Red defences at Längelmäki, 65 kilometres north-east of the town, while attacking along the north-western front at the same time. Some Red units collapsed and fled; others held their posts to the last. On the 24th the Whites cut the southern link at Lempäälä and on the 25th the western ones, encircling Tampere. The 1,000-strong Swedish Brigade of volunteers took part. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tampere)

The Battle of Tampere pitted 16,000 Whites against 14,000 Reds in Finland's first large-scale urban battle. The fight for the town began on 28 March, on the eve of Easter, at the Kalevankangas Cemetery, a day later remembered as "Bloody Maundy Thursday". The Whites, some of whose units lost more than half their men, failed to win a decisive victory and had to reorganise. In the early hours of 3 April, after a heavy artillery barrage, they broke into the centre and advanced house by house and street by street, reaching the eastern bank of the Tammerkoski rapids that evening. Red attempts to relieve the town from outside along the Helsinki–Tampere railway all failed, among them a 3,500-strong counterattack at Lempäälä led by Eino Rahja. The Reds lost the western parts of the town on 4–5 April, and the City Hall was among their last strongholds. The battle ended on 6 April with the surrender of the Reds in Pyynikki and Pispala. Fighting harder on the defensive, the Reds forced Mannerheim to commit the best-trained Jäger detachments he had been saving for Viipuri. The Reds had capable local commanders such as Hugo Salmela at Tampere, but they could not change the course of the battle. On the last night Aaltonen led a unit through the siege and escaped across the ice of Lake Näsijärvi. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tampere) [9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Aaltonen)

Tampere was the bloodiest battle of the war. The Whites lost 700–900 men, including 50 Jägers, the battalion's heaviest loss in any single battle of 1918. The Reds lost 1,000–1,500 killed and 11,000–12,000 captured. Seventy-one civilians died, mainly from shelling, and the eastern part of the town, built largely of wood, was completely destroyed. The Whites began executing surrendered Reds immediately. According to English-language sources, 1,000 Reds and 200 Russians, most of them soldiers, were executed after the battle. Leaflets in Mannerheim's name promised that prisoners would not be shot, yet one unit executed 20 surrendered Reds in the yard of the Näsinlinna palace. The prisoners were taken to a camp in the Kaleva district east of the centre, where 1,228 died of execution, disease or hunger over the next five months. According to some sources a mass grave at Kalevankangas Cemetery holds 2,751 Reds, 1,208 of them killed in action. After Tampere fell, the number of prisoners became too large for the Whites to go on shooting most captured Reds as before, and the war's first large camp was set up there. The defeat marked the beginning of Red Finland's collapse. On 8 April the People's Delegation left Helsinki for Viipuri, and on the 10th the Reds reorganised their whole administration, giving Kullervo Manner the supreme command and dictatorial powers. ## German intervention: from Hanko to Viipuri {finland germany}

Germany had not set its sights on Finland from the start. Finnish activists had repeatedly asked for German help since the February Revolution, but Germany, under pressure on the Western Front, did not want to jeopardise its armistice and peace talks with Soviet Russia. That changed on 10 February 1918, when Leon Trotsky broke off the talks at Brest in the hope of revolution in Germany. On the 13th the German leadership decided to retaliate by sending troops to Finland as well, inviting "requests for help" from Russia's western neighbours as a pretext; White Finland's representatives in Berlin duly made one on the 14th. Mannerheim wanted German weapons but opposed actual German intervention, trusting the Jägers and the demoralisation of the Russian army. The Vaasa Senate, however, relied on German military and political aid, and social liberals who had at first resisted it changed their minds as the war dragged on. The agreements of 7 March bound White Finland to the German sphere of influence. The German war leader Erich Ludendorff wanted to keep Petrograd under threat via the Viipuri–Narva area and to install a German-led monarchy in Finland. The Finnish Senate paid the full cost of the intervention and urged Finns to provide the German troops with food and shelter. According to Russian-language sources, Wilhelm II replied on 7–8 March that Germany would not wage war for Finnish interests against a Soviet government that had signed the Brest treaty, nor support Finnish military action beyond Finland's borders. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea_Division) [19](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE-%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D1%91%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%84%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D1%82_%281918%E2%80%941920%29)

On 5 March a German naval squadron landed on the Åland Islands, which a Swedish expedition had occupied since mid-February and left in May. On 3 April the 10,000-strong Baltic Sea Division under Rüdiger von der Goltz landed unopposed at Hanko, west of Helsinki; just beforehand Russian sailors scuttled four submarines in Hanko harbour. On the 7th Colonel Otto von Brandenstein's 3,000-strong detachment took Loviisa east of Helsinki. Russian-language sources put the total of German troops in Finland at 14,000–15,000. At dawn on 12 April 2,000–3,000 German soldiers attacked Helsinki from the north-west, while Vice Admiral Hugo Meurer's squadron blocked the harbour, shelled the southern districts and landed marines. Around 7,000 Reds held the Workers' Hall, the railway station, Smolna and the Senate area, but their best troops were on other fronts, and Helsinki White Guards who had been in hiding joined the Germans as they advanced. On the 13th the Germans pushed into the working-class districts and shelled the Workers' Hall, putting out the red lantern of the Finnish revolution; at about 2 p.m. a white flag went up on the tower of the Kallio church. Sixty Germans, 300–400 Reds and 23 White Guards were killed, and around 7,000 Reds were captured. The Germans held a victory parade in the city on the 14th, then pushed on through Hyvinkää and Riihimäki to Hämeenlinna on the 26th. At Hyvinkää at least 150 Reds were executed by the Whites after the battle. On 19 April Detachment Brandenstein took Lahti, cutting the western Red Guards off from the eastern ones. Between 22 April and 1 May several thousand western Reds and Red refugees tried to break through around Lahti on their way to Russia, but were held. Six hundred Reds and 80 Germans died, and 30,000 Reds were captured in and around the town. The long Red columns, which included women and children, suffered heavily under White attacks; for the Reds it was a "road of tears", for the Whites the sight of enemy caravans heading east was a moment of victory. Meanwhile the Whites turned to Viipuri, where 18,500 Whites faced 15,000 Reds. Having cut the Reds' link to Petrograd on the Karelian Isthmus on 20–26 April, they opened the final assault late on the 27th with a heavy Jäger artillery barrage, and in the early hours of the 29th took Patterinmäki, the symbolic last stand of the Red rising. Four hundred Whites and 500–600 Reds died, and 12,000–15,000 Reds were captured. The People's Delegation had already left for Petrograd by sea, and the flight of the leadership embittered many Reds. Haapalainen and Gylling stayed in Viipuri to organise its defence and escaped to Petrograd by motorboat in May. The last Red strongholds between Kouvola and Kotka fell by 5 May, and the war ended on the 15th, when the Whites took over Fort Ino, a Russian coastal artillery base on the Karelian Isthmus, from the Russian troops. On the 16th White Finland held a great victory parade in Helsinki led by Mannerheim. ## Terror and the prison camps {finland}

Both sides used executions as political violence, known in Finland as the White Terror and the Red Terror. It combined a calculated part of the war planned by commanders with local, personal killings and revenge. At least a third of the Red Terror and most of the White Terror was centrally directed. In February the White high command set up a Desk of Securing Occupied Areas and issued Instructions for Wartime Judicature, later called the Shoot on the Spot Declaration, which let field commanders execute essentially anyone they saw fit. According to Russian-language sources, on 25 February Mannerheim ordered that anyone offering "armed resistance to the lawful forces" or "carrying arms without the army's knowledge" be shot on the spot. No order authorising Red Terror by the less organised Red Guard leadership has been found. Many executions were carried out by mounted Flying Patrols of 10 to 80 youths aged 15 to 20 under an adult leader with absolute authority. The Reds executed influential Whites, politicians, landowners, industrialists, police officers, civil servants, teachers and White Guards, and killed ten Lutheran priests and 90 moderate socialists. Executions peaked in February, as the Reds secured power, fell in March, when they could not take new ground, and rose again in April as they prepared to leave Finland. The two main centres of Red Terror were Toijala and Kouvola, where 300–350 Whites were executed from February to April. During the battle for Viipuri a drunken band of Reds entered Viipuri County Gaol and murdered 30 White Guard prisoners. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [5](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%93%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%8F_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%B9%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%B2_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B8) [23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viipuri_massacre)

Comprehensive White Terror began with the general offensive in March, grew steadily and peaked at the end of the war; between late April and early May 200 Reds were shot a day. Its targets were Red Guard and party leaders, socialist members of parliament, local Red administrators and workers, and it was especially harsh on Russian soldiers who had helped the Finnish Reds. When Viipuri fell on 28–29 April, the Vaasa and Kajaani regiments of the White army killed people taken to be Russians at the Annenkrone fortifications, in the yard of Viipuri Castle and in the streets. Estimates range from some 50 to 500–600; Lars Westerlund puts the toll at 360–420. Thirty-seven of the dead were of other nationalities, Polish soldiers, Ukrainians, Estonians, Jews and Tatars. Most had no link to the Red Guards, and many had greeted the Whites as liberators. Mannerheim ordered an investigation and punishment when he heard of the killings on 2 May, and the next day Rudolf Walden telegraphed orders to prevent violence against innocent Poles, Ukrainians and Russians, but no one was ever charged. Overall figures differ slightly by source: English-language sources give about 1,500 victims of Red Terror and about 9,000 of White Terror, while another, citing the Finnish war victims database, gives about 1,600 and 8,100. White victims were recorded precisely; the number of Reds executed immediately after battles remains unclear. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viipuri_massacre) [24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_terror_in_Finland_and_the_Baltic_states_%281918%E2%80%931919%29)

When the war ended on 15 May, the Whites and Germans held about 80,000 Reds and their families, including, depending on the source, 4,700–5,000 women and 1,500 children, as well as some 8,000 Russians. Over the next two months they were moved from more than 60 small camps into 13 main ones, among them Suomenlinna, Hämeenlinna, Hennala at Lahti, Riihimäki, Tammisaari, Tampere and Viipuri. The Senate decided to hold prisoners until each one's role had been investigated. The war had wrecked agriculture, there was no central supply system, and parcels from families were banned until the end of August. In June 2,900 prisoners died of hunger, malnutrition-related disease or Spanish flu, in July 5,000, in August 2,200 and in September 1,000. At Tammisaari an average of 30 prisoners died each day in summer, a mortality rate of 34 per cent; elsewhere it ranged from 5 to 20 per cent. Deaths in the camps are estimated at about 12,500 (3,000–4,000 from Spanish flu), or 12,000–14,000 including executions, with a further 600 dying soon after release. Sexual violence against women prisoners long remained taboo. The Estonian-born Hans Kalm alone carried out more than 500 executions at Hennala, at least 200 of the victims women. Ali Aaltonen, captured near Lahti, was shot there by Kalm in May and buried in a mass grave of more than a thousand Reds. Of 1,482 children held in the camps, 104 died. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War_prison_camps) [9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Aaltonen)

Legislation for a Treason Court was enacted on 29 May, and 145 lower courts under a Supreme Treason Court examined some 76,000 cases. Sixty-eight thousand Reds were convicted, mostly of treason; 39,000 were paroled, and the rest served on average two to four years. Of 555 death sentences, 113 were carried out. The courts, working in the condemnatory atmosphere of White Finland, fell short of impartiality, and some innocent people were found to have been imprisoned. Before they were set up, more than 5,000 surrendered Reds had already been executed on the decisions of local courts-martial. In August Robert Tigerstedt, chief physician of the Tammisaari camp, wrote in a secret report that such a death rate had never been seen even in Tsarist Russia; Social Democrats leaked it to the Swedish press and it spread across the Nordic countries and to Britain. The wealthy businessman Hjalmar Linder visited Suomenlinna and wrote that "the Red madness has turned into a White Terror"; denounced as a Red sympathiser, he had to leave the country. In September the camps passed from the army to a civilian correctional office and nearly 40,000 prisoners were paroled, with 10,000 more pardoned in October; one English-language source also credits Svinhufvud with pardoning 36,000 Red prisoners that autumn. At the end of 1919, 4,000 remained; 3,000 were pardoned in January 1920 and civil rights were restored to 40,000 former Reds. The last 50 were pardoned in 1927 by Väinö Tanner's Social Democratic government, and only in 1973 did the Finnish state pay compensation to 11,600 former prisoners. ## From a planned kingdom to a republic {finland germany}

The Vaasa Senate returned to Helsinki on 4 May, but the capital was under German control. White Finland had in effect become a protectorate of the German Empire, and the White Army's quartermaster general Hannes Ignatius called von der Goltz "the true Regent of Finland". There was no armistice or peace negotiation between Reds and Whites, and no formal peace treaty ending the civil war was ever signed. On 18 May Svinhufvud became Protector of State, or Regent, and after he stepped down as chairman of the Senate on the 27th, Juho Kusti Paasikivi formed a conservative, monarchist Senate that asked the German troops to stay. Mannerheim clashed with the Senate over German hegemony and over his own plan to attack Petrograd, drive out the Bolsheviks and take Russian Karelia, and resigned as commander-in-chief on 25 May; the Germans opposed the plan because of their treaties with Lenin. Parliament became a rump: the Social Democrats, who had held 92 of 200 seats before the war, kept only a handful of deputies. In it the monarchists argued that the Swedish Instrument of Government of 1772 was still valid and the throne simply vacant; the republicans replied that the law had lapsed with the February Revolution, that parliament had assumed the Tsar's powers on 15 November 1917 and that a republic had been adopted on 6 December. When the republicans blocked a new monarchist constitution, the monarchists used the 1772 law to choose a king without amending the constitution. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Finland) [6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pehr_Evind_Svinhufvud) [20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCdiger_von_der_Goltz)

On 9 October, under German pressure, parliament elected Prince Friedrich Karl of Hesse, brother-in-law of Wilhelm II, King of Finland. Svinhufvud had even travelled to Berlin to ask the Kaiser for his son Prince Oskar; for him monarchy was a means of securing German support rather than a conviction. One deputy proposed the title "King of Finland and Karelia". But when the Kaiser abdicated on 9 November and the armistice was signed on the 11th, everything changed. The Allies made it known that Finland's independence would be recognised only if it abandoned its alliance with Germany. Warned by the West, the government of Prime Minister Lauri Ingman, himself a monarchist, asked Friedrich Karl to give up the crown, and the king-elect, who had never set foot in Finland, renounced it on 14 December. Von der Goltz and his division left Helsinki on 16 December. Svinhufvud stepped down and Mannerheim became Regent. Mannerheim had gone to Sweden in June and, meeting Allied diplomats in Stockholm, made plain his opposition to the government's pro-German policy; in October the government sent him to Britain and France to seek recognition. As Regent he secured it: the United States and Britain recognised Finnish sovereignty on 6–7 May 1919. The Western powers wanted democratic republics in post-war Europe to draw the masses away from revolutionary movements. Finland had turned from a monarchist protectorate of the German Empire into an independent republic. [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Finland) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Civil_War) [6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pehr_Evind_Svinhufvud) [7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustaf_Emil_Mannerheim)

The first local elections under universal suffrage were held on 17–28 December 1918, and on 3 March 1919 came the first free parliamentary election since the civil war. With the left and the socialists able to vote, the republican parties won three-quarters of the seats. At its first official congress after the war, on 25 December 1918, the Social Democratic Party committed itself to parliamentary means and disavowed Bolshevism and communism. The architect of the new constitution was Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg. Chairman of the Constitutional Committee since 1917, he supported a republic against the monarchists' constitutional monarchy throughout 1918 and kept redrafting the proposals, and his text was enacted as the Constitution Act on 17 July 1919. Regent Mannerheim, though a monarchist, ratified it. In the first presidential election, held in parliament on 25 July, Ståhlberg, backed by the Social Democrats, the Agrarians and the National Progressive Party, defeated Mannerheim by 143 votes to 50; Mannerheim had only the National Coalition and Swedish People's Party behind him. Ståhlberg was a moderate liberal reformer who favoured improving the material lot of workers and poor Finns. As president he pardoned most of the Red prisoners despite fierce criticism from the right, White veterans and senior officers, and signed laws giving trade unions equal standing with employers in collective bargaining and the Lex Kallio, which distributed land from large landowners to former tenant farmers and the landless. These reforms were meant to win even former Reds over to the democratic republic. ## Expeditions to the east: the heimosodat and the Petrograd question {finland russia estonia}

The Vaasa Senate's foreign aims went beyond defeating the Reds and ending Bolshevik influence: it also sought to extend Finland into East Karelia, home to Finnic-speaking peoples. According to Russian-language sources, Mannerheim swore at Antrea station on 23 February that he would not sheathe his sword until the last of Lenin's soldiers had been driven out of Finland and White Sea Karelia. East Karelia had never belonged to the Swedish Empire or the Grand Duchy. According to the historian Aapo Roselius, some 10,000 Finnish volunteers took part in the expeditions and uprisings of 1918–1922 that Finns call the heimosodat, the "kinship wars". The first was the Viena expedition of March 1918. Kurt Martti Wallenius's Jägers crossed the border at Kuusamo but got bogged down fighting Finnish Red Guards, and the conscripts mutinied once the operation went beyond the border. About 350 volunteers under Carl Wilhelm Malm reached Kem on the White Sea in April, fell back to Uhtua and tried to win over the villages one by one. The population was split between those wanting independence, those wanting autonomy and a small minority favouring union with Finland, and for most of them practical matters such as food came first. To keep Germany and its Finnish allies away from the White Sea and the Murmansk railway, the British landed at Murmansk and used a battalion of 1,400 Red Finns and a "Karelian Regiment" to guard the line; Oskari Tokoi became political adviser to this British-organised Murmansk Legion. The Finns in Viena withdrew on 2 October after defeats in August and September. In May a Petsamo expedition of about 200 volunteers had also been turned back by a force from the British cruiser HMS Cochrane. [28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heimosodat) [29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viena_expedition) [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petsamo_expeditions) [19](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE-%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D1%91%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%84%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D1%82_%281918%E2%80%941920%29) [3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskari_Tokoi)

In the summer of 1918 petitions to join Finland arrived from across East Karelia, above all from Repola, which had voted for union. The Finnish army occupied Repola that autumn, on 15 October according to Russian-language sources. In January 1919 a small volunteer force took Porajärvi but was soon pushed out by Bolshevik troops. In February Mannerheim told the Western powers and the Russian Whites that Finland would attack the Bolsheviks in Petrograd if it received material and moral support, and at the same time the Aunus (Olonets Karelia) expedition was prepared. Its commander, Gunnar von Hertzen, reckoned that 1,000 Finnish volunteers would suffice if the Karelians joined in. The 1,000 volunteers crossed the border on the night of 21 April, aiming for Lodeynoye Pole, Petrozavodsk and the Murmansk railway, took Olonets on the 23rd and for a time threatened Petrozavodsk. But there were too few troops and few Karelian volunteers. Two thousand more volunteers were recruited and Aarne Sihvo took command, yet on 20 June Paavo Talvela's regiment was beaten just outside Petrozavodsk by the Red Army and Finnish Red Guards. On 26 June more than 600 Finns from the Red Officer School in Petrograd crossed Lake Ladoga and landed at Vitele behind the Finnish lines, and the expedition fell back with heavy losses. Its only result was that Porajärvi declared in June for union with Finland and was occupied by the regular army. In July, on the southern Karelian Isthmus, Ingrian Finnish refugees proclaimed a Republic of North Ingria (Kirjasalo), which never held more than about 30 square kilometres. [31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunus_expedition) [29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viena_expedition) [19](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE-%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%BE%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D1%91%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%84%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BA%D1%82_%281918%E2%80%941920%29) [32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Ingria)

Finnish volunteers also crossed the sea to Estonia. After the 1st Finnish Volunteer Corps under Martin Ekström, the Sons of the North (Pohjan Pojat) raised by Hans Kalm, 2,213 men and 400 officials, crossed the Gulf of Finland on 12 January 1919. The Finnish committee had set a ceiling of 1,000 men, which Kalm ignored. They were thrown into the Battle of Paju on 31 January and in February crossed the border to take Marienburg in Latvia. Estonia's own war is covered in the event on the Baltic wars of independence. Petrograd itself, however, the Finns never marched on. Mannerheim saw the White victory in Finland as part of an all-Russian anti-Bolshevik struggle, but made recognition of Finnish independence by an authoritative Russian government the condition for an advance. In a telegram to the Allies of 4 June, Alexander Kolchak accepted Finland's independence only de facto, leaving recognition de jure to a future Constituent Assembly. According to Russian-language sources Mannerheim concluded a secret agreement on 18 June with Nikolai Yudenich, who was then in Finland, but it produced no practical result. Ahead of the presidential election the Social Democratic press seized on the Kolchak government's ambiguity to portray Mannerheim's friendship with "White Russia" as a threat to independence. Ståhlberg, who favoured peace with Soviet Russia, won the July election. When Yudenich's North-Western Army reached the outskirts of Petrograd in October, Mannerheim wrote that if the Whites were beaten Finland would bear the blame, but he no longer held office. ## The Treaty of Tartu of 1920 and after {finland soviet}

In 1920 the situation in the east changed sharply. After the Allies left northern Russia in the autumn of 1919 and the Whites collapsed, the Provisional Government of Karelia, which had resolved at Uhtua on independence for White Sea Karelia, was driven into Finland by the Red Army in May. On 8 June the Karelian Workers' Commune, an autonomous region of the Russian SFSR, was created at Petrozavodsk. Edvard Gylling stood behind the idea: head of the Communist Party of Finland's Stockholm bureau, he went to Moscow in May at Lenin's invitation to report on the feasibility of an autonomous Karelian republic. In the north, Wallenius led another expedition into Petsamo in January on the pretext of a request from Yevgeny Miller to reconnect a telegraph line, but a Soviet landing on 22 March forced it back towards Norway. In July the Red Army drove the Finns out of most of East Karelia, leaving them only in Repola and Porajärvi. The negotiations that opened at Tartu in June were led on the Finnish side by Juho Kusti Paasikivi, with Väinö Tanner, Väinö Voionmaa and Rudolf Walden among the delegates; the Soviet delegation included Platon Kerzhentsev. According to Russian-language sources, Foreign Minister Rudolf Holsti wanted a border running from Lake Ladoga through Lake Onega to the White Sea, while Paasikivi thought only territory whose inhabitants wished it should be joined. Finland proposed a referendum in East Karelia but dropped it in the face of Soviet opposition. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petsamo_expeditions) [37](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%82%D1%83%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%80_%D0%BC%D0%B5%D0%B6%D0%B4%D1%83_%D0%A0%D0%A1%D0%A4%D0%A1%D0%A0_%D0%B8_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B5%D0%B9) [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29)

After almost five months of talks, the treaty was signed on 14 October in the building of the Estonian Students' Society at Tartu. The border followed the old line between the Grand Duchy and the Russian Empire. Finland gained Petsamo with its ice-free harbour on the Arctic Ocean, which Alexander II had promised to Finland in 1864 in exchange for land on the Karelian Isthmus. In return Finland gave back Repola and Porajärvi, annexed and occupied after the Viena and Aunus expeditions, agreed to withdraw its troops by 14 February 1921, and handed North Ingria to Russia; the Soviet side in exchange promised cultural autonomy for East Karelia. The Soviets guaranteed Finnish merchant ships free passage from Finnish ports on Lake Ladoga via the Neva to the Gulf of Finland, and Finland guaranteed land transit to Norway through Petsamo. Finland agreed to disarm Fort Ino opposite Kronstadt and to demilitarise its outer islands in the Gulf of Finland. According to Russian-language sources the Central Executive Committee of the Russian SFSR approved the treaty on 23 October and the Finnish parliament on 1 December, and President Ståhlberg ratified it on 11 December; ratifications were exchanged in Moscow on 31 December. This treaty is distinct from the Treaty of Tartu that Estonia signed with Soviet Russia in the same town in February. Nationalists on the Finnish right called a treaty that gave up the dream of a Greater Finland shameful, but Paasikivi later admitted that the border was too good for Finland to last. [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29) [30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petsamo_expeditions) [31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunus_expedition) [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [37](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A2%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%82%D1%83%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D1%80_%D0%BC%D0%B5%D0%B6%D0%B4%D1%83_%D0%A0%D0%A1%D0%A4%D0%A1%D0%A0_%D0%B8_%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BB%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%B5%D0%B9)

The eastern border stayed restless after the treaty. When the Finnish foreign ministry ordered him to stop the people of Repola and Porajärvi from arming themselves, Bobi Sivén, the young police chief of Repola, shot himself on 12 January 1921, leaving letters that accused Finland of "betraying" the East Karelians. With promised autonomy poorly carried out and food scarce, East Karelian separatists rose in the autumn of 1921, joined by some 550 Finnish volunteers, mostly as officers and squad leaders. The Finnish government refused official involvement but did not stop volunteers crossing the border, and the Soviet side treated this as military intervention. Some 20,000 Red Army troops counterattacked and crushed the rising by February 1922, and about 30,000 East Karelian refugees crossed into Finland. In Russia the expeditions of 1918–1920 and the conflict of 1921–1922 are counted as a Soviet–Finnish war, while Finnish historiography does not regard the expeditions as wars against Russia. The Karelian Workers' Commune became the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1923, and Gylling, as chairman of its Council of People's Commissars until 1935, pursued a Finnish-language policy. Bringing in emigrants from North America and Finland to a region where Finns were a minority, it was condemned in the 1930s as "nationalist chauvinism"; Gylling was removed in 1935 and executed in 1938, and Eero Haapalainen was shot in Petrozavodsk in 1937. The border drawn at Tartu held until 1939, when the Soviet Union broke the treaty by starting the Winter War. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Karelian_uprising) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Gylling) [11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Haapalainen) [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tartu_%28Finland%E2%80%93Russia%29)

The war's very name is an interpretation. During the war both sides spoke of a War of Independence (vapaussota): liberation from capitalism for the Reds, freedom from Soviet Russian influence for the Whites. The Reds and their supporters also spoke of Class War and Revolution, the Whites of the Red Rebellion, and the Social Democrats rebuilt after the defeat increasingly used Civil War. In a 2008 survey of 1,005 people by the newspaper Aamulehti, 29 per cent chose Civil War, 25 per cent Citizen War, 13 per cent Class War, 11 per cent War of Independence and 5 per cent Red Rebellion. English-language sources put the dead at 35,000–38,000 out of a population of about three million, with some 15,000 children orphaned; most deaths occurred not on the battlefield but in the camps and the terror. Society split into "citizens of two nations": Whites were called "butchers" (lahtari), Reds "red Russkies" (punikki). Until the 1950s mainstream literature took the victors' view, and the Reds' story was told widely only after Väinö Linna's trilogy Under the North Star (1959–1962). Reconciliation came slowly. Kyösti Kallio appealed in his Nivala address of 5 May 1918 to rebuild a nation not divided into Reds and Whites, and Väinö Voionmaa lamented in 1919 that the young country had lost almost everything in the war. English-language sources see the Reds' defeat, the failure of most White goals and the simultaneous weakness of Germany and Russia as the basis of the Finnish compromise. The exiled leaders, meanwhile, founded the Communist Party of Finland in Moscow on 29 August 1918, and the suffering of the camps increased support for communism in Finland. body.en: The rump parliament elected Prince Friedrich Karl of Hesse King of Finland; he renounced the throne on 14 December.

body.en: The Finnish army occupied Repola in East Karelia, which had voted to join Finland (date from Russian-language sources).

body.ko: 스빈후부드가 물러나고 만네르헤임이 섭정이 되었다. 폰 데어 골츠의 사단은 16일 헬싱키를 떠났다.
body.en: Svinhufvud stepped down and Mannerheim became Regent; von der Goltz's division left Helsinki on the 16th.

body.ko: 한스 칼름의 「북방의 아들들」 2,213명이 핀란드만을 건너 에스토니아 독립전쟁에 뛰어들었다.
body.en: Hans Kalm's 2,213-strong Sons of the North crossed the Gulf of Finland to join the Estonian War of Independence.

body.ko: 의용병 1,000명이 동카렐리야로 들어가 23일 올로네츠를 차지했지만 6월 말 물러났다.
body.en: 1,000 volunteers entered East Karelia and took Olonets on the 23rd, but fell back at the end of June.

body.ko: 17일 정부 형태법이 공포되었고, 25일 의회는 스톨베리를 143표 대 50표로 초대 대통령에 뽑았다.
body.en: The Constitution Act was enacted on the 17th, and on the 25th parliament elected Ståhlberg first president by 143 votes to 50.

body.ko: 페트로자보츠크에 러시아 소비에트 연방 사회주의 공화국의 자치주가 세워졌다. 에드바르드 귈링이 그 구상을 제안했다.
body.en: An autonomous region of the Russian SFSR was set up at Petrozavodsk, on a plan put forward by Edvard Gylling.

title.en: Treaty of Tartu between Finland and Soviet Russia

body.ko: 핀란드는 페차모를 얻고 레폴라와 포라얘르비에서 철수하기로 했으며, 소비에트 측은 동카렐리야의 문화적 자치를 약속했다.
body.en: Finland gained Petsamo and agreed to leave Repola and Porajärvi; the Soviet side promised cultural autonomy for East Karelia.
